title: About
text:
My name is William Reddien; I am a current undergraduate student at Davidson College in the class of 2029 studying Computer Science and Data Science, and I am very passionate about my work.
I developed this website while abroad in Germany on Davidson College’s Dean Rusk travel Grant as part of my project studying the eagle as it appears on ancient coins. This website houses all of the other projects, programs, databases, and evaluations I wrote and developed while abroad as part of my project, and serves as a digital portfolio whose development helped me learn and increase proficiency in many data science skills (and whose existence stands as a testament to those skills).
I am a proficient SQL and R programmer, and am likewise skilled not only in base Python but the pandas library. I have experience with most fundamental tools in Excel, and am currently expanding that facet of my repertoire.
Previously I’ve worked as an intern in two positions— as a lab intern at MIT I used R to visually create and analyze data drawn from cellular activity, and as a market research intern with a Texas law firm I evaluated potential clients as well as developed and set into motion effective ways to initiate partnerships and relationships with them.
As a member of the “Cats’ Stats” club at Davidson, I’ve spent a substantial amount of time analyzing the data surrounding not only Davidson’s men’s basketball team but simultaneously our opponents, building scouting reports on the strengths and weaknesses of both teams and players, and prescribing strategies that lead our team to victory.
When I’m not working, programming, learning a new skill, or looking at coins, I spend most of my time running, playing and designing video games, reading and writing, watching movies, or with my friends.

w.reddien@outlook.com
Or, reach out to me via LinkedIn

title: Price Regression Model and Auction Data
text: In the modern day ancient coins are a commodity and a collector’s item, despite or perhaps enhanced by their value as historical artifacts. As such, the prices of ancient coins are some of their most interesting features — what monetary value a theoretically ‘worthless’ coin has in the modern day can be effectively attributed to what somebody is willing to pay for it.

title: Eagles ‘The Adler’ And Money Across The World
text:
Introduction
Throughout history, eagles have appeared all over coinage. The earliest Greeks and Romans minted the bird somewhat randomly, but over time it grew to have clear symbolic meaning. Or more accurately, it meant a number of very different things to almost every people of nearly every location, time, and culture it appeared in. But despite how varied its meaning was (and still is), it persevered through the Roman imperial period, and is still a very common piece of iconography on the coins of myriad modern countries.
Take for example two ancient eagles, and two modern eagles:
The eagle was an incredibly common symbol on both Ptolemaic Imperial and Roman Imperial coinage, but their meanings were starkly different. On early Ptolemaic coinage, the eagle represented a divine authority and connection to Alexander the Great, while on the Roman Imperial coins it represented Roman virtues.
And in the relatively modern day, the eagle on Mexican pesos is representative of the historical myth of Mexico’s founding, while on American coins it represents liberty, and freedom.
My name is Will Reddien— I am a data and computer science student at Davidson College. This summer (2026), courtesy of Davidson’s Dean Rusk international experience grant, I am spending six weeks in Germany investigating the influence of ancient Greek and Roman coinage on the modern coinage of Europe, and the world. Last semester I wrote a paper on the eagle as it appears and changes on coins in the Davidson coin collection, and so this summer I’m continuing my investigation by looking at museum collections, Munzkabinetts, and local coin shops around Germany (and some in neighboring countries). While I travel, I’m building up my own small dataset of all the eagle coins I see, which will be posted and analyzed on this website when I’m done with it.

title: Data, Museums, And Eagles Across The World
text:
The Project
As this project grew in scope a number of new goals arose for me, on top of those I originally pursued. In order to chase those new ideas, though, I needed to commit a substantial amount of time to not only learning but applying skills as a data analyst.
During my first few days in Germany I built a roadmap with goals for the trip. I went on to complete all of these goals, despite the fact that I constantly changed ideas or added new ones to the list as the trip progressed. My goals were as follows:

Build a dataset from the coins I see that feature eagles.
Learn about the cataloging process of ancient coins and how it differs between different collections, as well as study how different collections and museums present their coins — then, write about the positives and negatives that come with different methods.
Train an image classification model to discern coins with eagles from coins without eagles.
Develop a price prediction model for ancient coins via linear regression and historical auction data.
Launch a website to display everything I develop: My datasets and their analysis, maps of eagle coin mintings throughout history, the models I’ve built, and what I learn about cataloging, sourcing, and presentation of coins through collections and museums.

The launch of this website marks my final objective complete. At this point all of the other goals on the list are complete and can be found/interacted with in different pages on this site. It’s important to note, though, that each of these overarching goals was secretly a number of smaller objectives, so even the seemingly simple ones required a number of different skills and steps to complete.
Along with my analysis, the datasets I built/sourced can be found throughout the website’s pages, free for you to scroll through if so desired. If something seems missing that you wish you could access, the github repo for this site is linked in the upper bar of every page and is publicly accessible, so please feel free to look through it.

title: Price Regression Model and Auction Data
section: Building a Dataset from Auction Data
text:
Building a Dataset from Auction Data
As part of my analysis of all things eagle-coin related, I took data from the Classical Numismatic Group, LLC.’s online research database of historic auctions in order to analyze some recent price data. All of the auction data was manually entered into an excel spreadsheet by me, in the format seen below, and converted into a .csv file. I selected 200 eagle-coins all minted before 300 AD (with one exception) and sold after 2020, and then logged the relevant data from their entries— This included sold price, material, condition, minting location, and date of creation. Because of lack of quantity of coins from specific mints, I generalized the mints into larger regions. Likewise, many of the coins I documented were listed as being minted between a range of dates— in those cases, I entered the date as the average date from within that range for the sake of simplicity.

And here, you can explore the auction data dataset yourself:






The variables I chose to add are the most important variables in deciding a coin’s value, and most often it’s the combination of multiple rare traits that makes a coin uniquely valuable— for instance, coins minted under Cleopatra VII are incredibly expensive, but if they are in poor condition they tend to be cheaper. Likewise a common bronze coin might be graded Extremely Fine, and ergo be worth more than a coin that might typically be rarer.

title: Price Regression Model and Auction Data
text:
Initial Findings and Visualizations
Before building the price predictor I want to first show some interesting visuals I developed from the dataset, which will help provide context for the prediction model.
The first visual is a bar chart with the number of coins that were sold at different price points— looking at it you can clearly see a right-skew, with most of the coins being sold at around $100-$200. There were a few exceptional coins with much higher prices, although fewer and fewer as the price grew.









The vast majority of the coins were graded Fine, Near Very Fine, and Very Fine, leaving only a bit of room for coins at other condition levels. As a result, in this boxplot the trend is the strongest in the lowest grades, but you can still see how the price generally increases as the condition goes up. The boxes that appear only as lines are representative of the limited number of entries with those grade levels. Note also the range of sold prices for Near VF and VF in particular.









Here are two visualizations of how many coins in the dataset there are for each condition level, to put the previous plot even more into context: Note: The rating system for coin condition in this dataset, starting at Near Fine, is this: Near Fine -> Fine -> Near VF -> Very Fine (VF) -> Near XF -> XF (Extremely Fine) -> Choice XF -> AU


















Lastly, here’s a histogram showing how coins in the dataset were minted over time. The y axis measures the number of occurrences of dates within the timeframes noted on the x axis, and the colored sections of the chart indicate what portion of coins from a given era came from each region.
The distribution is somewhat bimodal, or even potentially trimodal with the highest points being between 300 and 200 BC (mostly from Alexandria/the Ptolemaic Empire) and between 200 and 300 AD.
Ignoring the single post-300 AD coin, there’s a weak, but present positive linear relationship between chronology and quantity of eagles. Although this is based on my small auction dataset, it is generally representative of the same trend we can see in larger datasets.

title: Price Regression Model and Auction Data
text:
Price Prediction Regression Model
The major project I’ve been able to create by collecting this auction dataset is a regression model that predicts the value of an ancient coin based on the variables in my auction dataset. This model, created through multiple linear regression, predicts a coin’s value based on what values have been inputted for each variable.
For example, based on the model a very fine bronze eagle coin from north Africa minted in 200 BC could be expected to sell for about $170.
It’s important to note that while there is almost certainly strong correlation between many of these variables and price, because of the limited number of datapoints in the dataset and the fact that many of the variables are categorical, a completely accurate linear prediction model is not reasonably possible. However, the model was created in the same way a larger (or more numerical) dataset would be developed.
Take a look at this: The plot of residuals against the fitted linear model.









Some explanation of the image: Right now, the model maps the difference between actual price data from the dataset and the price predicted by the model on the Y-axis as points, while the x-axis represents the prices of the coins.
The predicted model is very clearly nonlinear here, making a sort of U shape. The shaping of the model indicates that a linear model is not a good predictor for this dataset. Normally this is a bad sign, but take a look at where the majority of the data is:
The U shape is effectively divided into three sections— an initial decreasing section, a flat middle section, and an increasing third section. In the case of our data, the vast majority of the residuals are strongly correlated with the slightly negative linear trend in the first third of the model.
Additionally, look at the shape the residuals make over time: The residuals start closely tied to the model, and spread out over time in a shape almost like a cone or megaphone. This is a phenomenon known as heteroscedasticity, and its presence here indicates that when predicting coins at low price points the model is highly accurate— however, as price predictions get high the model’s accuracy decreases drastically.
It’s also important to note that this model is limited by the fact that coin prices cannot drop below $0.
Here’s another visual, which fixes our spread issue and makes the model a bit more linear:









By taking the log() of the sold_price category in the original model, we can approximate a somewhat more linear and significantly more evenly distributed regression model. This does change the meaning of the plot, though, and its distribution still isn’t incredibly even.
The y-axis here represents percentage errors between the predicted prices and actual prices. This means that a point at 0.1 on the y-axis had a price 10% higher than what the model predicted.
The x-axis is a little bit more complicated, but it can be effectively understood as a squished or shrunken down version of the previous x-axis. Each of the numbers on the x-axis, when used as the exponent on ex to undo the log function, will be equivalent to some dollar value. Basically, a coin at 6 is more expensive than a coin at 5 by a lot (e6 vs e5 USD), a coin at 5 is more expensive than a coin at 4 by a smaller margin, and so on and so forth.
Onto a Q-Q plot, which we’ll create for both the original and log/modified linear data. First the original:









And the log data:









In both graphs we can see some variance from the theoretical line on the tail ends, particularly at the higher end of the range. This is generally expected since the data, as we saw above, is strongly right skewed. This effect is slightly reduced in the Q-Q for our log model, although it is certainly still present.

title: Price Regression Model and Auction Data
data
Price Regression Model and Auction Data
text:
Regression Accuracy and R Squared
The last real indicator of accuracy we can look to is the R squared value for the regression model— or, the percentage of variation in the price values that can be reasonably explained by the regression model. In the case of the log-modified regression model our multiple R-Squared value is 0.3466, meaning the model developed from my dataset can explain about 35% of the variation in price values. This means much of the variance is unaccounted for, something which could be remedied with a much larger dataset.
Overall, this model is relatively effective at predicting low price coins, but fails when estimating for coins of higher prices. This comes directly as a result of the fact that the data is significantly right skewed— with more data from higher value coin sales the issue could certainly be resolved.
Although price prediction for coins is achievable, many of the sold coins listed on even CNG’s website were sold for values much higher than the group’s own prediction model, illustrating the difficulty in developing price predictions for a market where new, unique artifacts are introduced constantly.

Image Classification Model
text:
In researching coinage for this project I encountered an issue I didn’t expect to find: poor documentation. It made sense that the coins I tracked down in local shops may not have had all of the information I’d have liked to have seen, but during my trip I visited several museums which displayed coins without any given information. Documentation for every coin in a museum installation may be too high an ask, especially when coins are not a major selling point for a site, but several displays still managed to shock me. As I discuss in another webpage, I encountered one displayed coin that had been incorrectly identified, which was particularly shocking.
I couldn’t help but wonder, though, since many of these smaller museums did not have their collections displayed online, if perhaps the difficulty and time-commitment that comes with identifying and documenting every individual coin in a collection was a limiting factor. I know from experience that very few tools exist that can accurately identify coins, and none that I know of for free. At some point during this project, I had the idea to build (or at least attempt to build) that tool myself.
As a proof of concept, I used images from the MANTIS coin database to train a neural network that can identify eagle-coins.

title: Image Classification Model
text:
Results



















These images are the responses the model gave to four inputted images of coins, and contain those images as well as the model’s assigned label. As seen in the four images above, the model is relatively accurate at identifying whether images of coins feature eagles or not (which tracks, based on the 80% success rate). The first three images are labeled correctly, with the first two coins featuring eagles and the third featuring a temple. The fourth however is incorrect, with the model labeling it an eagle when it is in fact not. Understandably so, though, as the image does seem somewhat eagle shaped.
While it is not perfect, based on the dataset it can at the very least successfully identify eagles that fit into the most typical design archetypes with high success, even if it still trips over trickier images and some non-eagle coins.
I consider this project a huge success— I learned how to build, test, and train image classification software at a small scale, and develop scalable skills that could be applied in the future to a much larger database.

title: Image Classification Model
text:
Future Developments
While I would love to increase the size of my dataset drastically and train my model even more, I am limited by my timeframe and current skill level. If I continue developing this model, I will work on increasing my count of images, epochs, and training runs to first increase its accuracy until it reaches about 97%. Simultaneously I would build a more advanced dataframe that contains archetypes of eagles from specific societies and time periods, which I would train the model to identify once its base eagle identification skill was strong enough.
One final development I would want to make would be training the model on the names of rulers within each previously trained society and era, and potentially use information on the minting series of that ruler to have the model identify a top 3-4 series’ a given coin could be from.
This would be very time-consuming even with automatic methods such as scraping, and as such I will likely never reach that final phase of development on my own. However, it might be reasonable to build a new dataset with coins for a specific empire, for example the Seleukid Empire, and train the model to identify coins first based on empire, then ruler. This would be logistically much easier for me to develop alone, and could serve as an even better proof of concept for an all-encompassing classification model.
While I cannot include the classifier directly on this website without going through a third party or purchasing my own server, I have included the .pt script for the program on the github repo for this website.

title: Image Classification Model
text:
Development Process
To start, I invested a significant amount of my spare time into reading webpages and watching lectures on the fundamentals of machine learning and reinforcement training, including but not limited to the recordings of lectures from fast.ai. Once I had a strong fundamental understanding of the concepts, I specifically dove into lectures covering image classification models.
One of the most important concepts I discovered was transfer learning, which allowed me to use a basic pre-existing classifier, and build my identifier from a foundation of already complete training. Transfer learning is the industry standard, with it cutting hours of training from the development of a model. I decided that, given my timeframe and other project goals, transfer learning was the best approach.
Since many tutorials for creating image classification models already exist, I was able to learn the basics of what I needed very quickly (thanks to Pytorch for the brilliant documentation). I loaded in a simple test dataset from the internet, and began experimenting with a pre-existing classifier.
Once my test case model had learned from the previous model and was completely trained with the simple dataset, I began the training process with my coin data.
For this project I used images I collected manually— reasonable since my model is only a proof of concept, although to develop an applicably useful level of accuracy an automated approach would be better. I selected 51 images of coins prominently featuring eagles and 50 coins without eagles, specifically choosing about 7 images I suspected the model might struggle with for each category. I split each group into my ‘training’ and ‘value’ folders, with each folder subdivided into eagles and non-eagles. The training folder contained most of the images, leaving the value folder with ten of each image type to act as a key or point of reference for the model during training. Importantly, the way that I built this structure made the program scalable, so in the future if I wanted to develop this model further I would be able to easily add more categories, images, and keys.

I then began training the model. I ultimately went through two phases of training, with 25 epochs each. Training the model asks it to take each image in the training folder and make a prediction based on what it already knows about my images. After it makes a prediction for the entire dataset, it reports its accuracy score and repeats the process. After all 25 passes through the dataset, the model saves the weights derived from its most accurate attempt so that it can improve upon itself in future training runs.
The first attempt was not clean, resulting in a 65% accuracy rating. This is expected since my dataset is not large enough to reach industry standard accuracy ratings, so 65% accuracy on the first run was relatively a huge success. I did encounter an issue early in the process with the sizes and formatting of my images, but was able to improve the model such that it can reformat and resize images to be assessed in a standardized manner.
The second run of training went faster than the first, and saw much higher accuracy at a best score of 80%. This is about the highest I could have hoped for with such a small dataset, so this second round marked the project as a success.
Finally, I ran a third session of training— which saw no improvements. Again, though, because of the small size of my dataset this was expected; with only ~100 total images the best accuracy a model like this can achieve should be about 80%.

title: On Professional Cataloging and Coin Displays
text:
In displaying coins for public consumption there are many different possible approaches an organization can take. Some of these approaches, particularly in physical museum exhibits, are entirely under the control of some curator or collector, while the responsibility associated with others can be attributed to catalog organizers or researchers. It also happens that the possibilities of presentation both physically and digitally can be limited by a collection’s cataloging process, with limited information in a catalog constraining a collection’s options for display.
Through visiting a number of museum exhibitions as well as searching through and engaging with a variety of digital collections, I have experienced a huge spread of different approaches to coin presentation, and as such have come to appreciate certain features just as I shudder when I see others. Following my German experience, I have concluded that not only are there right and wrong ways to display coinage, many museums do not know how to present coinage effectively— to the extent that both aficionados and general consumers lose out on valuable information.

title: On Professional Cataloging and Coin Displays
text:
Museum Exhibits - Physical Presentation Methods
One thing that really surprised me while visiting museums was how wildly different their coin displaying strategies were, even among the higher calliber establishments. I saw everything ranging from well grouped, methodically organized and informational displays to a museum that did not have any physical coins despite their website claiming that they did (much to my disappointment). Beyond museum displays, the presentation of coins in local shops was, less surprisingly, a completely different experience.
While this range was certainly present throughout all the exhibits, the organizations focused specifically on coins such as the Muenzkabinetts vastly outranked the average museum in terms of effective organization. Shockingly, though, what I consider the best display I encountered over the course of my travels— even outranking the coin-focused organizations— was a local museum’s exhibition.
The worst coin display I visited was by far the Fortress Museum in Salzburg, which noted on their website the presence of Roman coins, but actually had zero coins! The only coin related section of the museum that I was able to find was a stand with photos of some coins connected to the museum, but even those were not Roman. In terms of the sort of ranked organizational structure I have organized the museums by, the Fortress museum is in the lowest level, that being ‘tier five’.









Salzburg’s coin display. Note that these are only images of coins, and no actual coins are present








In tier four, standing just above the Fortress Museum’s non-existent display in my ranking are the Colombischloessle in Freiburg, the Neues Museum in Berlin, and the Strasbourg Archaeological Museum— all museums which did feature some coins, although in a manner with which I was starkly disappointed. There seems to be a common strategy in coin presentation of ‘put all the coins in a pile behind glass such that visitors can see that there are coins, but can get no useful information out of them.’









Two examples of display strategies at the Colombischloessle

















One of the few displays I spotted in Strasbourg







An exemplary Neues Museum display





Unsurprisingly, I am not a fan of this tactic, since it means I must spend substantial amounts of time trying to glean identifying characteristics from a coin, time which could otherwise be spent learning about that same coin or developing other projects— in fact, this very issue is what inspired me to develop a small, but accurate image classification model, which I discuss in the Data Analyses and Models section of this website.
Strasbourg’s museum was the biggest offender of this non-display tactic, but it was present to some smaller extent in several of the other museums I was able to visit. The Colombischloessle employed the tactic in a few areas, but did have some more effective display tactics employed throughout itself.
The third tier of coin exhibit was one I only encountered in the Museum Luzern, which had a surprisingly well organized albeit compact coin display which effectively presented much of the museum’s collection. The Museum Luzern’s coins were organized into a gridlike pattern in a series of drawers, each of which featured a barcode— upon scanning the barcode, a screen above the coins would present information about a given coin. Similarly arranged coins were present elsewhere in the museum, although unfortunately this second section did not feature a supplementary digital catalog.









Both sections of coins at the museum Luzern, featuring me








While museum-goers were limited to viewing only one coin’s information page at a time, the tightly packed nature of the Museum Luzern’s extensive collection of relics and objects of interest meant their coins would inherently need to be compactly presented, and as such the coins were presented about as effectively as possible. Additionally, I am a big fan of digital information tabs for coins in physical museums (as I discuss later on this page), and as such I appreciated their system. However, the presence of coins in their museum as a whole suffered from a handful of flaws— firstly, while they evaded the ‘non-display’ method of coin presentation I previously mentioned, there were other smaller coin displays scattered around the museum which suffered from being hard to study due to lying horizontal behind a vertical glass barrier. Additionally, as far as I observed, these other coins were not substantially documented within the museum itself, leaning more towards that non-display mention they nearly avoided (even with the coins themselves being generally more easily studied).









Examples of the Bode-Museum’s displays and informational keys








Next we move on to ‘Tier two’, the first level of museums with a specific focus on coinage— the Bode-Museum, Staatliche Muenzsammlung Muenchen, and Dresden Muenzkabinett all fell into this rank. These museums all featured robust collections of coins that were well organized, all displayed such that it was possible to see the coins, and with information cards regarding every coin with key defining facts (for example minter, or date) such that one who wishes to learn more about a coin is able to find it online and efficiently do so.









A display example from the Staatliche Muenzsammlung in Munich








The approach taken by each of these three collections was slightly different, and I do have to say that even within this one ‘level’, the Dresden Muenzkabinett was by far the frontrunner. Dresden featured not only an early coin pressing machine, but displays including paper money, strange materials coins were made from, and (my personal favorite) coins with nicknames. Unfortunately, because of how Dresden presented the information it had about its coins, as well as the fact that they gave no solution to the issue of only one side of a coin being visible when on display, it fell into the second tier of collection for me. Each of these museums had something different to offer, from magnifying lenses that allow you to see more precise details on coins to the previously mentioned variety of unusual but interesting displays.









The Dresden Muenzkabinett
















Finally in the top tier there stands only one museum, a site which I spontaneously decided to visit but which was by far the best collection I was able to explore, even outranking the coin-specific museums— the Basel Historical Museum. The Basel Historical Museum had not one, but two distinct areas of coin presentation. While the lesser of the two, there was an installation focused on ‘treasure hoards’ that unfortunately suffered from many of the same flaws as the tier four collections. But! On the flipside, Basel’s main display was undoubtedly the greatest coin display I have ever seen.









The ‘Treasure Hoards’ exhibition





Basel’s primary exhibit regarding coins was the perfection of a coin display, with rows of coins organized not only chronologically (which was generally the case for all other high tier displays), but by key features. For example, while there were areas dedicated to different time periods and rulers, there was also a section specifically regarding eagles on coins— obviously this was a key point of interest on my end, but in general these smaller sections of display massively enhanced the quality of the collection.
Perhaps even more importantly, every section of display had a corresponding digital micro-catalog, which not only provided tangible and well-researched information about each coin, but allowed visitors to see high quality photos of both the obverses AND reverses of the coins on display. While I’ve only briefly mentioned it previously there is a very distinct and seemingly insurmountable challenge in displaying coinage, that being having both the obverses and reverses of coins visible simultaneously. Unfortunately, only one side of the coin can be visible at a time, meaning much of a coin’s intrigue and valuable information are rendered inaccessible to collection visitors. This issue was of particular note during my expedition, since many coins that could have potentially featured eagles were displayed on their obverse sides.









The primary Basel coin display











Museums have taken a number of approaches to remedy this— some simply ignore it, others display coins facing either direction, and others have opted to display two of the same coin next to one another with each coin facing a different direction. There is even a strategy where coins are suspended vertically, such that visitors can walk around an exhibit and view a coin from both sides. The best and most effective solution, in my opinion, is the approach taken by Basel, which is to allow users to easily and quickly find the digital display, which not only allows them to see both sides simultaneously but allows a more detailed analysis of the side previously visible.

title: On Professional Cataloging and Coin Displays
text:
Cataloging - Digital Information and Consistency
In terms of the crossroads between online coin catalogs and museum displays— despite what I originally presumed— overlap seems to be generally minimal. While very large collections feature online catalogs (an example being the Bode-Museum), most of the smaller museums I visited did not commonly feature their coins online.
For the most part this lack of online documentation is a minute detail, since most of the coins featured in smaller museums belong to series’ that can be found online other sources, but it is concerning to me that potential coin data is being left unaccounted for due to what seems to be largely inconvenience, as well as a dearth where one large collaborative database should be.
While to an incredibly small scale in an incredibly focused topic, I am trying to achieve some online presence of this otherwise undocumented data, such that hopefully it can be used in the future if needed by classicists, data analysts, or anybody else interested in these coins.

section: How I Corrected an Incorrect ID
text:
How I Corrected an Incorrect ID
As noted above, the Museum Luzern’s exhibit in particular had a handful of poorly identified or described coins. For the most part this wasn’t an issue, since there was enough information on display that more interested museum-goers could use to track down and learn more about any particular coin. However, one coin in particular caught my attention as I scanned through the collection.
The coin in question had been identified as an eagle minted under Ptolemy II, which happens to be one of the specific series’ of coinage I have extensively researched. I had been visiting the museum with a friend, and upon reading the description of the coin I immediately noted to him my vague sense of distrust in that particular page of documentation. I pulled up some reference images, since this alleged Ptolemy II coin looked dissimilar to those I had seen before, but upon finding some that looked a bit like it I initially dismissed my concern.



A typical Ptolemy II eagle


Fast forward to about a week later in Berlin, when I was working on identifying the coins I had taken photos of in the Museum Luzern to add to my evergrowing dataset. As I went through the eagle coins one by one, I had no trouble finding matches in one database or another for each of their types— that is, except for one. While the “Ptolemy II” coin I had flagged as suspicious was similar in design to some legitimate Ptolemy II coins, it didn’t exactly match any of the coins I was able to find minted under its alleged ruler. And the closer I looked, the more I realized that the coin had a number of features that distinguished it completely from the coins of Ptolemy II.
The most important distinction was the text written on the coin— not only did the writing itself not match any text on Ptolemaic coins, but the completely vertical structure of the words was a giveaway. Even with the most vertical inscriptions of Ptolemy II’s coins, the text always curved to follow the edge of the coin at the top of the design. Below is one of those coins.

Also note that the head on the obverse, while seemingly wearing a somewhat unorthodox crown, is actually a radiate head, something never seen under Ptolemy II. The clues that I found helped me narrow my search, and after a more difficult identification process than I had anticipated, I was finally able to correctly identify the coin as a bronze of Antiochus VIII. Here is the MANTIS documentation for the coin:
https://numismatics.org/collection/1944.100.76816



The misidentified eagle in question


Following my successful identification, I wrote a message (in German) to the Museum Luzern’s contact email explaining my concern with the identification, as well as providing evidence for my updated ID and what that ID was. I have emailed a number of website-listed emails in the past to radio silence, so I assumed that my email would be the last update to this story. But lo and behold, about a month later I received this reply:

Guten Tag Herr Reddien


Herzlichen Dank für diesen Hinweis.


Gerne werden wir dem nachgehen und falls nötig Korrekturen vornehmen.


Freundliche Grüsse
Which loosely says ‘Hello. Thank you for the info, we’ll look into this and update it if needed.’

title: On Professional Cataloging and Coin Displays
text:
Learning to Display Coins Correctly
In truth, there is no perfect way to display coins— at least not that I have seen. And aside from the museums I visited on this journey I have either seen online, heard about, or visited museums using other strategies to display coins. I had the amazing opportunity previously to visit the Museum of the Romans in southern France, which featured a giant angled display of coins with a movable magnifying glass visitors could use to look more closely at individual artifacts. I’ve heard about another museum, I believe also in France, which displays coins vertically in glass cases extending from kitchen island-style exhibits, such that observers can move around the display to see both sides of the coins. I’ve even been to museums with exhibits simply titled ‘Roman Coins’, where the noted coins are sitting conglomerated in a visually impressive but informationally useless pile.
There is a middle ground of display— coins shouldn’t be piled indistinguishably in heaps, but over-organization can be draining to mentally absorb. My perfect display (in a semi-cliche manner) combines features from several museums I’ve seen, and is modeled based on the most effective features from each.
Firstly, my coins would be organized based on chronology and geography— I would have individual sections of display for major time periods, with subsections present for specific distinguishing features, such as minting region. For example, early Greek coins would generally be together, but coins from the empires the rose following the death of Alexander the Great would be sub-grouped by their individual empire/region— the Ptolemies and Egpyt/North Africa would comprise one subsection, while the Seleukids in Asia Minor would another. This style of organization would make the collection more digestible to observers partially through more of the context surrounding each coin being brought to the forefront, but also partially due to the side effect of visually similar coins being more closely associated with one another. And on the flipside, if coins vary especially wildly within one time period, for example the early Greeks, a point of interest will be created for the observer, who might question why so much variation existed in such a small geographic region. This method of presentation will also organize the coins in a more easily navigable way for coin-enthusiasts, who could search for coins in the display almost like shelves in a library organized by not only genre, but author, country of origin, or date of creation.
The only exception to this would be some smaller, more focused sections of the display. For example, shocking nobody, I would love to have a smaller display focused on coins featuring eagles across the world. Taking heavy inspiration from the Dresden Muenzkabinett, I would love to have sections like their ‘coins of interesting materials’, or ‘coins with nicknames’. These would likely be either in a separate room from the main collection (as in Dresden), but could be interspersed into the primary display rooms based on space availability (as with the cabinets in Munich)
Lastly, the most important element: physically, how would I perfectly display coins? In short, I would learn from Basel’s strategies and display my coins in cases with only one side up, but with digital interfaces attached to each case (or group of cases) which could be used to find more information about individual coins as well as high quality images of their faces. The unfortunate nature of coins is that only one side can be seen at a time, and I do have some complaints with a number of the display methods that attempt to combat this. Firstly, having two copies of a coin side by side with each facing one way is interesting and on paper effective, but as an observer I feel that it devalues each individual artifact. Part of what makes these ancient coins so interesting is how they have survived, meaning in what state. The cracks on two coins will never be the same, nor the grime on the edges, or even the exact shape. While I would love to see two sides of the same coin simultaneously, I would rather those two sides be of the exact same coin, and not two separate, albeit very similar ones.
I likewise wouldn’t even consider the vertical walk-around-to-see-both-sides display style, largely since the walking bit is inconvenient. As an avid runner I have no gripe with moving, but interrupting my study of a coin to move to its other side is an immersion breaker that I believe siphons much of the fun and intrigue out of the coin learning experience, and makes observation of more than a couple coins feel like a chore. I do think that this method has potential to be great for smaller displays, or even if the coins could be somehow made to rotate such that viewers wouldn’t need to move, but as of now I would not include it in my museum.
Another reason I would choose to use digital interfaces is because, for the most part, they do not wear down. The Staatliche Muenzsammlung in Munich featured a large, printed paper index of cards for each display case of coins— which didn’t feature very much information about the coins, although that was another gripe— and while these indexes were fine and clearly legible, they did not seem new. A digital screen would of course have to be maintained just as paper indexes would, but would come with a large variety of other benefits, including the fact that it is easily updatable, and for the most part always feels new. Unless of course its software was written in the 20th century, which felt like it was the case for the Museum Luzern (despite how much charm that added to the display).

title: conclusions
text:
My (brief) Discussion with a Curator
When I originally set out to complete this project, I had grand hopes of meeting with curators or collection managers, studying in studiensaals, and learning about where every coin each collection comes from through discussions with figureheads. Unfortunately, though I reached out to a number of institutions (and ultimately visited many of them), I did not receive a single reply, even upon following up. While I am generally disappointed with this, I was still able to achieve almost all of what I set out to do, and as such the detail seems minute.
However, I did have one chance to talk for only a few minutes with a curator of the Staatliche Muenzsammlung in Munich. After spending quite a bit of time in the collection I realized that it was almost its closing time. I was leaving, but fortunately as I was walking towards the door, I ran into a man I didn’t catch the name of, but who I was told by the desk attendant was one of the experts on the museum. I spoke to him briefly in German, and was thankfully able to ask him a handful of questions I had prepared in advance just in case this happened.
Through our very brief discussion, I was able to learn a number of things about Munich’s collection. Firstly, they do actively purchase coins even to this day, despite the collection being over 500 years old. This was also notable, since the curator mentioned that buying coins was their primary way of acquiring new artifacts (as opposed to donations or from archaeological excavations). The museum has a digital catalog (which I had already engaged with), and it is updated to include all new acquisitions. While I speak and read German relatively effectively, I couldn’t determine what some of the displays were, in particular several giant, ornate cases. The curator explained to me that they were the boxes in which the coins had been stored leading up to the modern day, hence the existence of the collection for 500 years.
We talked a bit more briefly about the collection, but only a bit longer since he seemed to be busy. I had learned what I needed, though, since purchased coins (as you might expect, and as I learned through creating my auctiondata dataset) are highly documented, and thus, combined with their digital catalog, seems to be extensively and observably documented, in such a way that I am able to learn a great deal about their documentation style by engaging with their digital system.

title: The Hidden Coins of Shops and Local Museums
text:
Data regarding ancient coins is lost almost constantly for a variety of reasons— even at the modern ‘source’, people steal coins from archaeological digs and sell them in secrecy, meaning we lose data as to what hoard they might have been a part of, or where they were actually found. One of those reasons, though, is completely avoidable, simply being the fact that many of the coins that have been documented by individual collectors or that are featured in small museums or sold in coin shops do not have their data entries accessible online.
Not to say that online documentation of coins is a requirement for having a collection, but when so much data is left on the cutting room floor, one wonders if any potential use was lost. Especially with many collections being considered and documented independently, it feels as though some combination of collections in a mass digital catalog could fill in gaps in our knowledge about less studied or less common coins. I sought to remedy this issue, at least to a small extent, through this project, and I believe that at least as a proof of concept the I have been successful.

title: The Hidden Coins of Shops and Local Museums
text:
Development Processes
As noted before, throughout this trip I visited a variety of local and large museums, along with both coin-focused shops and general antique stores in search of undocumented coins. Thankfully, while coin collecting is relatively popular in Germany there were a tangible, finite number of shops in each city for me to visit. Each time I visited a shop, I scanned through their catalog looking for ancient coins, and especially ancient coins with eagles on them— of course, one complete comprehensive dataset would be the ultimate goal of an expanded version of this project, but my focus during this trip was primarily eagalic coins if only because I think they are especially interesting.
Once I was in a shop and had identified some coins of interest, I checked first for what documentation was listed with the coin (often very little to none other than a price), took a photo of one or both sides of a coin when possible, and wrote down any other information that could be helpful for later identification. As I visited more and more shops I became better and better at this, and was even able to see some behind the counter coins (even when they weren’t especially of interest).
I performed a similar process when visiting museums, moving slowly through their collections looking for coins with visible eagles. Unfortunately (as I note in my page on coin cataloging and display) it is effectively impossible to know if a coin has an eagle on its non-visible side without knowing every coin in the museum, and as such it is inevitable that some coins were missed using this approach. Regardless, I wrote down the usually helpful information regarding the museums’ coins, and took photos of their faces.
Finally, after visiting a museum, shop, or collection and gathering the information needed, I would begin the process of identifying the coins myself by cross referencing their designs and information with those of various digital catalogs such as MANTIS and CRRO. After an identification process of a difficulty somewhere between instant identification and a 1 hour wild goose chase, I documented the vital information I found about each specific coin in an Excel master spreadsheet based on whatever reference coin I found. Now, after repeating this process for each coin hotspot, I have built out a fully documented collection of coins which fords the boundaries between officially presented and somewhat underground coins— a collection which can be accessed on this very webpage.









Some examples of the coins I saw at various shops and street markets

title: The Hidden Coins of Shops and Local Museums
text:
The Matter of Eagles
Tragically, while many of the shops I visited while abroad did feature interesting classical coins, many of which I photographed, almost none of their ancient coins featured eagles (despite eagles being an especially common feature on their stocks of coins beyond the Greco-Roman period). As a result, because my project focused nearly exclusively on classical eagalic coinage, I was not able to successfully identify any coins to add to my database. As mentioned on other pages of this website, shops were also few and far between, further decreasing the potential eagles I could find.
One shop I visited did list one eligible coin on their website— that shop in particular being the Berlin location of the chain of coin shops ‘AM’. The location that I visited, where I was directed to the website, unfortunately did not have the particular coin I noted in stock, and so I neglected to include it in my dataset.
While the nature of this project’s limited scope decreased the amount of potential coins, a future expedition with an expanded objective would undoubtedly see success (as evidenced by the myriad eagle coins I spotted from beyond my timeframe, as well as other ancient coins in general).

title: The Hidden Coins of Shops and Local Museums
text:
View the Dataset
It is important to note that this dataset is essentially a micro-scale example of what an expanded version of this project could set out to achieve. As such, while all of the coin identifications are accurate in regard to certain fixed attributes such as type designs and minting authorities, mutable features such as weight should not be taken as 100% accurate.
All points in the dataframe are copied directly from the MANTIS or CRRO database, and as such are occasionally not up to the standards of my typical documentation. While I would have liked to rewrite all the type descriptions to be standardized and generally more descriptive, I decided preserving the coin’s attributes as they have been professionally documented would be the best approach for this project.

title: The Hidden Coins of Shops and Local Museums
text:
Unidentifiable Coins
A handful of coins that I photographed should theoretically be included in my dataset, but have unfortunately been snubbed due to how difficult identifying them has been. This came as a bit of a surprise to me and only afflicted three of the coins I photographed, but unfortunately I have as of yet been unable to find a proper identification for a few coins. But why?
While it is true that most of the coins I photographed had proper IDs in their respective collections, these IDs are not always as helpful as they seem. One particularly difficult coin that I managed to identify was listed in its collection as being minted in ‘Bruttium’. Bruttium is an ancient region in southern Italy, and as such this completely tracks— except, not all digitally documented coins list all of their attributes. The ‘Bruttium’-labeled coin was minted in a city within Bruttium, with its digital entry listing the minting location as that city rather than ‘Bruttium’ as I had seen in the museum. Thankfully, there was still enough information available in the museum to help me identify the coin. However, I had also photographed a second coin from Bruttium with much less supplementary information to ground my search in.
A similar predicament has come to pass for two other coins I intended to include in this dataset, meaning that (though I wish it were not so) as of yet they have been obfuscated.

title: Conclusions
text:
Ultimately this project was a raging success. Out of the goals I set out to achieve (as listed on the main webpage) I have completed them all, with the launch of this website marking the final goal complete. Throughout this experience I was able to explore not only large museums but local shops while I built my own cross-collection comprehensive dataset of ancient eagle coins.
Through my own research and work documenting coins, as well as investigating large collections, I was able to gain a substantial understanding of the variations in coin cataloging both online and in a physical presentation. In the ‘Data Analyses and Models’ section of this site, you can experiment with and see how I both developed a linear regression price prediction model for ancient coins, and trained an image classification model to identify the presence of eagles on coins.
And finally, this website, which showcases not only the projects I developed, but everything I learned along the way.
As the project comes to a close I am becoming increasingly satisfied with the work that I have done, and I am incredibly thankful to have been given the opportunity to pursue this passion project.

title: Conclusions
text:
Into the Future
I briefly touched on future goals for this project in other website pages, but as the project comes to a close all I can think about are more ideas to add to it. I spent quite honestly too much time while working on this project trying to find or make a complete dataset of the ~36,000 eagle coins MANTIS features in their database so that I could develop more resources with it. While that goal has been paused for the sake of time management, that dataset would be the first thing I create in a continuation of this project. Thankfully, after learning and experimenting with Python’s pandas, I have the tools necessary to (if very tediously) build this dataset myself.
Along with that dataset, I would like to create an interactive map, such that as a user changes a date input eagle coins from around that time period begin to appear and disappear, creating a visual of where eagle coins were being minted and when.
I would also love to expand the scope of certain parts of this project beyond just ancient eagle coins, to include coins of different time periods or non-eagalic ancient coins. While I find eagle coins in particular to be very fascinating, my universal dataset would be much more applicable if it featured a comprehensive database of all classical coins, and not just those with eagles.
As mentioned on my image classification model page I would love to continue development on that front as well, potentially building my training dataset such that the program could identify eagle coins of different eras, different materials, or different locations.
Even beyond what I’ve just mentioned there is so much more to be added, and while this project has been limited in both timeframe and scope, a future iteration would be an incredibly exciting project to lead. With the infrastructure now laid out, the project could be expanded through more of Europe, including collections from cities much closer to the heart of Rome leading to so much valuable information being included. One day, if this project continues to grow, it could change the way modern numismatics operates and expedite our understanding of the ancient world.



In the Staatliche Muenzsammlung Munich

About the Site, and Myself
My name is William Reddien; I am a current undergraduate student at Davidson College in the class of 2029 studying Computer Science and Data Science, and I am very passionate about my work.
I developed this website while abroad in Germany on Davidson College’s Dean Rusk travel Grant as part of my project studying the eagle as it appears on ancient coins. This website houses all of the other projects, programs, databases, and evaluations I wrote and developed while abroad as part of my project, and serves as a digital portfolio whose development helped me learn and increase proficiency in many data science skills (and whose existence stands as a testament to those skills).
I am a proficient SQL and R programmer, and am likewise skilled not only in base Python but the pandas library. I have experience with most fundamental tools in Excel, and am currently expanding that facet of my repertoire.
Previously I’ve worked as an intern in two positions— as a lab intern at MIT I used R to visually create and analyze data drawn from cellular activity, and as a market research intern with a Texas law firm I evaluated potential clients as well as developed and set into motion effective ways to initiate partnerships and relationships with them.
As a member of the “Cats’ Stats” club at Davidson, I’ve spent a substantial amount of time analyzing the data surrounding not only Davidson’s men’s basketball team but simultaneously our opponents, building scouting reports on the strengths and weaknesses of both teams and players, and prescribing strategies that lead our team to victory.
When I’m not working, programming, learning a new skill, or looking at coins, I spend most of my time running, playing and designing video games, reading and writing, watching movies, or with my friends.
